text:
Chapter One: The Lantern
Mara found a blue lantern beneath the bridge. Its glass was cold, though a tiny flame moved inside. On the handle someone had carved the name Orin. She wrapped it in her red scarf and carried it home.

Chapter Two: The Visitor
At midnight a traveler knocked on her door. He had lost something near the river, he said, and could not return to the hills without it. Mara remembered the name on the handle. When she asked whether he was Orin, the traveler smiled. She returned the blue lantern, and he left her a map of the hills.

Niko planted three apple seeds beside the garden wall. Every morning his sister Ada brought water in a yellow jug. Only one seed grew. Through summer they sheltered the little tree from the wind. Years later, when its branches shaded the wall, Niko and Ada shared its first three apples and remembered the yellow jug.

The clockmaker kept a silver key in his left pocket. No clock in town required that key. One rainy afternoon, a child brought him a wooden bird whose wings would not move. The clockmaker recognized his father's carving. He took the silver key from his left pocket, wound the bird, and listened as it sang an old familiar song.

Captain Iva promised to return before the first winter storm. Her brother placed a white stone on the pier to mark the promise. Autumn passed slowly. On the last calm evening, a small sail appeared beyond the island. Iva stepped ashore, picked up the white stone, and placed it in her brother's hand.

The oldest book in the library had no title. Its first page showed a picture of a door, and its last page showed a key. Lina spent the whole afternoon reading the pages between them. At closing time she understood: the door was the library itself, and the key was the courage to ask a question.

A small dog waited at the station each Tuesday. The conductor called him Pepper because of his speckled coat. In spring, a woman stepped off the morning train carrying an empty leash. Pepper ran toward her. The conductor waved goodbye, pleased that the dog's long wait was finally over.

Eli built a little boat from a fallen branch and painted its sail green. He let it drift toward the bend in the river. Downstream, his cousin caught the boat beside an old willow. She wrote a note on the green sail and brought it home. That evening they planned a larger boat they could build together.

The guide told Tomas to remember the three crooked pines. They marked the safe path down the mountain. When mist covered the ridge, Tomas could no longer see the village. He waited until the wind moved the mist, found the three crooked pines, and followed the path beneath them all the way home.

Every Friday, Rosa baked one extra loaf of bread. She left it on the windowsill for whoever needed it. One morning she was too ill to open the bakery. By noon, neighbors had brought soup, flowers, and a warm loaf to her door. Rosa learned that a small kindness can find its way back home.

Juni named the brightest star over the barn Silver Bell. Her father explained that it had another name on his old chart, but Juni liked hers better. On their first night in a new house, she looked out of the window and found Silver Bell again. The sky had brought a little piece of home along with them.

The violin case contained a folded letter and a length of blue ribbon. Before each concert, Sera tied the ribbon to her wrist. The letter was from her grandmother, who had taught her the first four notes. Years later Sera gave lessons of her own, and began every lesson with those same four notes.

A fox with a white tail visited the orchard at dusk. The farmer did not chase it away, for it never harmed the hens. One evening the fox stopped at the fence and barked until the farmer followed. Beyond the gate, a lamb had fallen into a ditch. The farmer lifted it out, and the white-tailed fox disappeared into the trees.
